title: Java Modifiers
learningObjectives: Explain how access modifiers control member visibility.
Distinguish public, private, protected and package-private access.
Identify non-access modifiers such as static, final and abstract.
Use private fields with public methods to control access.
Choose modifiers that express intended class and member design.

understand.concept: Modifiers change the visibility or behaviour of classes and members. Access modifiers include public, protected, private and package-private access. Non-access modifiers include static, final and abstract, each expressing a different design constraint.
understand.whyItMatters: Appropriate modifiers help define a class's public API, protect implementation details and prevent unintended changes or extension.
understand.analogy: Think of a well-designed object as a small service with a clear responsibility: it keeps the information it owns and exposes only the operations other code needs.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a design aid; Java access, inheritance and dispatch follow the language's exact rules.

explain.narrative:
## Access modifiers

`public` allows access wherever the declaring type is accessible. `private` restricts access to the declaring top-level class. `protected` supports package access and subclass access under Java's rules. With no access modifier, package-private access applies.

## Non-access modifiers

`static` associates a member with the class. `final` prevents reassignment of a variable, overriding of a method, or extension of a class depending on where it is used. `abstract` marks incomplete classes or methods that subclasses must implement.

## Use the narrowest access needed

Expose only the operations callers need. Keep internal fields private and provide methods when controlled access is appropriate.

## Common mistakes

- Treating protected as simply public.
- Assuming final makes an object's contents deeply immutable.
- Using static when per-object state is required.

examples.title: Private field with public getter
examples.code:
class Profile { private String name = "Mina"; public String getName() { return name; } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(new Profile().getName()); } }
examples.explanation: The private field is accessed through a public method.

examples.title: Static member shared by class
examples.code:
class Config { static int version = 2; }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(Config.version); } }
examples.explanation: The static field is accessed through the class name.

examples.title: Final variable cannot be reassigned
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { final int limit = 10; System.out.println(limit); } }
examples.explanation: A final local variable can be assigned once.

examples.title: Protected member accessible in same package
examples.explanation: A subclass can access the inherited protected member.

examples.title: Abstract class requires implementation
examples.explanation: The concrete subclass implements the abstract method.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small Java program about java modifiers. Predict its output, then compile and run it with JDK 21.
practise.independentTask: Build an original program demonstrating java modifiers in a practical scenario. Include at least two test cases, expected outputs and a short explanation of your design choices.
hints: Identify the class, object or type that owns each piece of state or behaviour.
Trace the declared type and runtime object separately when inheritance is involved.
Compile after each small change and compare actual output with your prediction.
practise.challenge: Extend one java modifiers example with a realistic boundary case and explain how the design handles it.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier restricts a member to its declaring class?
questions.explanation: private provides the narrowest member visibility.
No access modifier gives package-private access.

questions.prompt: What does static indicate for a method?
questions.answer: The method belongs to the class
options: The method belongs to the class

questions.prompt: What does final prevent when applied to a method?
questions.explanation: A final method cannot be overridden by a subclass.

questions.prompt: What does abstract indicate for a method?
questions.answer: It has no implementation in that declaration
options: It has no implementation in that declaration
questions.explanation: An abstract method requires a concrete implementation in a suitable subclass.
